goals: Explain how nationalism and imperialism raised tension in Europe
Describe the armament race and the two rival blocs
Explain how the Sarajevo crisis became a general war

slides.heading: Why did Europe go to war in 1914?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — four **long-term causes** and the **immediate cause** at **Sarajevo**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: nationalism, imperialism, the armament race, the rival blocs, and the Sarajevo crisis of 1914
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In nineteen fourteen the great powers of Europe went to war with one another, and the war spread across the world. Why did it happen? In this part we study four long-term causes, nationalism, imperialism, the armament race and the rival alliances, and then the immediate cause, the murder at Sarajevo.

slides.narration: This timeline shows the main dates. Germany took Alsace-Lorraine in eighteen seventy-one. The Triple Alliance came in eighteen eighty-two and the Triple Entente in nineteen hundred and seven. The war began in nineteen fourteen, the fighting ended in nineteen eighteen, the Treaty of Versailles was signed in nineteen nineteen, and the League of Nations began work in nineteen twenty.

slides.heading: Aggressive nationalism
slides.body_md: Each nation put its **own greatness** above peace.

rows: Wish to recover Alsace-Lorraine, lost to Germany in 1871
Clashed with Austria-Hungary in the Balkans
Ambition for German dominance in Europe
Wished to unite Serbs living under Austria-Hungary

visual.alt: Table of forms of nationalism before 1914: French revanche over Alsace-Lorraine, Russian and Balkan Pan-Slavism against Austria-Hungary, German Pan-Germanism, and Serb nationalism against Austria-Hungary

slides.narration: Nationalism means love of one's nation, but before nineteen fourteen it often became aggressive. France wanted revenge for losing Alsace-Lorraine. Russia saw itself as protector of the Slav peoples, which brought it into conflict with Austria-Hungary. Germany dreamed of dominance, and Serb nationalists wanted to unite Serbs living under Austrian rule.

slides.heading: Imperialism
slides.body_md: Rivalry for **colonies**: the **Moroccan crises** of **1905** and **1911**.

rows: Colonies for raw materials, markets and prestige
Suspicion and near-war among the great powers

visual.alt: Table about imperialism: colonies were sought for raw materials, markets and prestige; Germany as a late-comer wanted a larger share; the Moroccan crises of 1905 and 1911 set Germany against France; the result was suspicion and near-war
visual.caption: Imperialism in four lines.

slides.narration: Imperialism means seeking colonies for raw materials, markets and prestige. Britain and France already held large empires. Germany, a late-comer, wanted a bigger share. Twice, in nineteen hundred and five and nineteen eleven, Germany and France clashed over Morocco, and Europe came close to war.

slides.heading: The armament race
slides.body_md: The **Dreadnought** (1906), **conscription** and war plans.

rows: Britain launched the Dreadnought (1906); Germany built similar ships
Conscription gave the continental powers millions of trained soldiers
Plans assumed rapid mobilisation once a crisis began
Fear, suspicion and readiness to use force

visual.alt: Table of the armament race: the naval race after the Dreadnought of 1906, conscript armies on the continent, war plans built on rapid mobilisation, and the resulting fear and readiness to use force

slides.narration: The powers also raced to arm. After Britain launched a powerful battleship called the Dreadnought in nineteen hundred and six, Germany built similar ships. On the continent, conscription gave countries millions of trained soldiers, and war plans assumed rapid mobilisation. This spread fear and made leaders ready to use force.

slides.heading: Quick check: Morocco
slides.body_md: True or false: Germany and France came into conflict over Morocco in 1905 and 1911.
slides.narration: Recall the two crises in North Africa. Were they about Morocco?

slides.narration: By nineteen hundred and seven Europe was divided into two armed camps. The Triple Alliance joined Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy. The Triple Entente joined Britain, France and Russia. Each power promised to support its partners, so a quarrel between two states could pull in all the others.

slides.heading: How the Entente formed

visual.alt: Flow of how the Triple Entente formed: the Franco-Russian alliance of 1894, the Entente Cordiale between Britain and France in 1904, the Anglo-Russian understanding of 1907, completing the Triple Entente
visual.caption: From isolation to the Entente.

slides.narration: Britain had long stayed out of European alliances. France and Russia allied in eighteen ninety-four. Worried by German ambitions, Britain settled its quarrels with France in the Entente Cordiale of nineteen hundred and four, and with Russia in nineteen hundred and seven. That completed the Triple Entente.

slides.body_md: Plan a **3 + 3 + 4** answer on the long-term causes.
bullets: (i) Nationalism: Alsace-Lorraine, Pan-Slavism, Pan-Germanism.
(ii) Imperialism: colonies, Germany's demand, Morocco.
(iii) Armament race: navies, armies, plans, and why it made war likely.

rows: Colonial rivalry; Germany's demand; Moroccan crises
Navies; armies; plans; why it made war likely

visual.alt: Worked example table planning a ten-mark answer on causes: three points on nationalism, three on imperialism, and four on the armament race
visual.caption: Plan before you write.

slides.narration: Here is a plan for a ten-mark answer in three parts. For nationalism, give three facts: Alsace-Lorraine, Pan-Slavism and Pan-Germanism. For imperialism, give three: colonial rivalry, Germany's demand and the Moroccan crises. For the four-mark part, describe navies, armies and war plans, then explain why they made war more likely.

slides.heading: Sarajevo, 28 June 1914
slides.body_md: The **immediate cause**: the murder of the **Archduke**.

rows: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, and his wife
Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist
Austria-Hungary had annexed Bosnia in 1908, angering Serbia

visual.alt: Table about Sarajevo: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, and his wife were killed at Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia, on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist; Austria-Hungary had annexed Bosnia in 1908

slides.narration: On the twenty-eighth of June nineteen fourteen, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, and his wife were shot dead at Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia. The assassin was Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist. Austria-Hungary had annexed Bosnia in nineteen hundred and eight, which had angered Serbia.

slides.heading: From Sarajevo to world war
slides.body_md: A **chain** of declarations in **six weeks**.

nodes.label: 28 July: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia
Germany declares war on Russia and France; invades Belgium
4 August: Britain declares war on Germany

visual.alt: Flow of the July crisis of 1914: the Archduke killed at Sarajevo on 28 June; Austria-Hungary sends Serbia an ultimatum; declares war on 28 July; Russia mobilises; Germany declares war on Russia and France and invades Belgium; Britain declares war on Germany on 4 August
visual.caption: From one murder to a general war in six weeks.

slides.narration: Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and sent it a harsh ultimatum. When Serbia did not accept every demand, Austria-Hungary declared war on the twenty-eighth of July. Russia mobilised to protect Serbia. Germany declared war on Russia and France and marched through neutral Belgium. On the fourth of August Britain declared war on Germany.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: immediate and long-term causes
slides.body_md: Correct the claim that "Sarajevo alone caused the war".
bullets: Point 1: Sarajevo was the **spark**, the **immediate** cause.
Point 2: the **fuel** was already there: nationalism, imperialism, the armament race and the blocs.
Tip: always separate **immediate** from **long-term** causes.

nodes.label: 28 July: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia
Germany declares war on Russia and France; invades Belgium
4 August: Britain declares war on Germany

visual.alt: Flow of the July crisis of 1914: the Archduke killed at Sarajevo on 28 June; Austria-Hungary sends Serbia an ultimatum; declares war on 28 July; Russia mobilises; Germany declares war on Russia and France and invades Belgium; Britain declares war on Germany on 4 August
visual.caption: From one murder to a general war in six weeks.

slides.narration: A common mistake is to say that the murder at Sarajevo alone caused the war. Correct it in two points. First, Sarajevo was only the spark, the immediate cause. Second, the fuel was already there in the long-term causes: nationalism, imperialism, the armament race and the rival alliances. Keep the two kinds of cause separate.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: nationalism, imperialism, the armament race, the blocs of 1882 and 1907, and Sarajevo as the spark
visual.caption: Part 1 in five lines.

slides.narration: To sum up Part One. Aggressive nationalism, rivalry for colonies and the armament race made the powers suspicious and ready to fight. The Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente divided Europe into two camps. The murder at Sarajevo on the twenty-eighth of June nineteen fourteen was the spark, and the alliance system turned a local quarrel into a general war.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Triple Alliance **1882**: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy.
Triple Entente **1907**: Britain, France, Russia.
Sarajevo: **28 June 1914**, **Franz Ferdinand**, **Gavrilo Princip**.
Britain entered on **4 August 1914** after Germany invaded **Belgium**.
Separate the **immediate** cause from the **long-term** causes.

slides.narration: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on the twenty-eighth of June nineteen nineteen in the Palace of Versailles near Paris, exactly five years after the murder at Sarajevo. Its terms were drawn up by the victorious Allies. Germany was presented with them and had to sign.

slides.heading: War guilt and reparations
slides.body_md: **Article 231** and **payments** for war damage.

nodes.label: Article 231: Germany accepts responsibility for the war

visual.alt: Flow of the financial and moral terms: Article 231 makes Germany accept responsibility; reparations for war damage follow; the peace was dictated without negotiation; lasting resentment in Germany
visual.caption: Guilt, payment and grievance.

slides.narration: Under Article two hundred and thirty-one, the war-guilt clause, Germany had to accept responsibility for the war and the losses it caused. On this basis Germany was required to pay reparations for war damage. Because the peace was dictated without negotiation, these terms left deep resentment in Germany.

slides.narration: The military terms were meant to keep Germany too weak to attack its neighbours. Its army was limited to one hundred thousand men, and conscription was banned. Germany could have no air force, only a small navy and no submarines. The Rhineland, next to France, was demilitarised, with no German troops or forts.

slides.narration: Germany also lost land. Alsace-Lorraine went back to France. The Saar was placed under the League for fifteen years, with its coal mines given to France. The Polish Corridor gave Poland a route to the sea and cut off East Prussia. Danzig became a free city, and all German colonies became mandates.

slides.narration: The idea of an association of nations to keep the peace was put forward by President Woodrow Wilson of the United States. The League's Covenant was written into the peace treaties of nineteen nineteen, and the League began work in January nineteen twenty, with its headquarters at Geneva in Switzerland.

slides.heading: Objectives of the League
slides.body_md: **Peace**, **collective security**, **arbitration**, **disarmament**, **cooperation**.

visual.caption: Objectives of the League (paraphrased).

slides.narration: The League aimed to maintain peace and security. Its members promised collective security, acting together against any aggressor. Disputes were to be settled by arbitration or judgement, not war. It also worked for disarmament, for international cooperation and for fair conditions of labour through the International Labour Organisation.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Putting **Italy** in the Triple Entente (it was in the **Triple Alliance**).
- Calling Sarajevo the **only** cause (it was the **immediate** cause).
- Mixing up **28 June 1914** (Sarajevo) and **28 June 1919** (Versailles).
- Saying the League had its own **army** (it had none).
- Placing the League in **New York** (that is the United Nations; the League was at **Geneva**).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one point per mark; the 4-mark part often asks you to explain or evaluate.

questions.stem_md: The Triple Entente was completed when Britain reached an understanding with Russia. In which year did this happen?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1907. The Anglo-Russian understanding of 1907 completed the Entente. 1882 is the Triple Alliance, 1894 the Franco-Russian alliance, and 1914 the start of the war.

questions.stem_md: Why did many French people before 1914 want to recover Alsace-Lorraine?

options.text_md: Germany had taken these provinces from France after the war of 1870–71
They had been sold by France to Britain

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Germany had taken these provinces from France after the war of 1870–71. Germany took Alsace-Lorraine after defeating France in 1870–71. The wish to win them back (often called revanche, meaning revenge) kept French–German hostility alive.

questions.stem_md: The idea that all Slav peoples of eastern and south-eastern Europe should stand together, with Russia as their protector, was called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Pan-Slavism. Pan-Slavism sought the unity of Slav peoples under Russian protection, which brought Russia into conflict with Austria-Hungary in the Balkans. Pan-Germanism sought the union of German-speaking peoples.

questions.stem_md: The crises of 1905 and 1911 between Germany and France arose mainly over control of which North African country?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Morocco. Both crises were over Morocco, where Germany challenged French influence. They show how rivalry for colonies (imperialism) brought the powers close to war.

questions.stem_md: Britain launched a powerful new battleship called the Dreadnought in 1906. Which cause of the war does the race that followed best illustrate?

options.text_md: The formation of the League of Nations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The armament race. Germany answered by building similar ships, and each side kept adding warships. This naval rivalry is part of the armament race before 1914.

questions.stem_md: How did the division of Europe into two armed camps make a general war more likely?

options.text_md: It forced every country to disarm completely
It placed Europe under a single government
A quarrel between two states could draw in their allies, turning a local conflict into a wider war

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A quarrel between two states could draw in their allies, turning a local conflict into a wider war. Because each power was bound to support its partners, a dispute in one corner (such as the Balkans) could pull in all the allies. The blocs did not lead to disarmament or remove rivalries.

questions.stem_md: Italy was a member of the Triple Alliance, yet it did not fight beside Germany in 1914. Which statement best explains this?

questions.stem_md: How did nationalism, imperialism and the armament race together prepare the ground for the First World War? Give one point on each.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the long-term causes of the First World War.

(i) Explain how aggressive nationalism created tension in Europe. **[3]**
(ii) How did imperialism add to the rivalry among the great powers? **[3]**

questions.solution_md: Nationalism; imperialism; armament race and its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) France wished to recover **Alsace-Lorraine**, lost to Germany in **1871**. **Pan-Slavism** made Russia the protector of Balkan Slavs, against **Austria-Hungary**, while **Pan-Germanism** encouraged German ambitions. Each nation placed its own greatness above peace.

(ii) The powers competed for **colonies** for raw materials and markets. **Germany** wanted a larger share than it held, which alarmed **Britain** and **France**. Crises over **Morocco** in **1905** and **1911** brought them close to war.

(iii) The continental powers built huge **conscript armies**, and Britain and Germany raced to build battleships after the **Dreadnought** of **1906**. Military plans assumed quick mobilisation. This spread **fear and suspicion**, encouraged leaders to rely on **force**, and meant that once a crisis began, armies were ready to march at once.

(i) The **Triple Alliance** (**1882**): **Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy**. The **Triple Entente** (completed **1907**): **Britain, France and Russia**.

(ii) Britain had long stayed out of European alliances. Alarmed by **German** naval and colonial ambitions, it settled its differences with **France** in the **Entente Cordiale** (**1904**) and with **Russia** in **1907**, completing the Entente.

questions.stem_md: On which date was Archduke Franz Ferdinand assassinated at Sarajevo?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 28 June 1914. The assassination took place on 28 June 1914. Britain entered the war on 4 August 1914, the armistice was signed on 11 November 1918, and the Treaty of Versailles on 28 June 1919.

questions.stem_md: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, killed at Sarajevo, was the heir to the throne of which empire?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Austria-Hungary. Franz Ferdinand was heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary. His murder by a young Bosnian Serb gave Austria-Hungary its reason to act against Serbia.

questions.stem_md: Who fired the shots that killed the Archduke and his wife at Sarajevo?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Gavrilo Princip. Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist, fired the shots. William II was the German emperor; Clemenceau and Wilson were leaders at the peace conference.

questions.stem_md: Why were Serb nationalists hostile to Austria-Hungary at the time of the Archduke's visit to Sarajevo?

options.text_md: Austria-Hungary had joined the Triple Entente

questions.stem_md: What did Austria-Hungary do on 28 July 1914, after Serbia did not accept its ultimatum in full?

options.text_md: It signed a peace treaty with Serbia
It asked the League of Nations to judge the case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It declared war on Serbia. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914. The League of Nations did not yet exist.

questions.stem_md: Germany's plan to attack France required its armies to march through a neutral country. Which country was it, and whose entry into the war followed?

options.text_md: Switzerland; Italy declared war on Germany
Belgium; Britain declared war on Germany

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Belgium; Britain declared war on Germany. German troops entered neutral Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed. Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914.

questions.stem_md: Why did Russia begin to mobilise its army after Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia?

options.text_md: Russia saw itself as the protector of the Slav peoples, including the Serbs
Russia was a member of the Triple Alliance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Russia saw itself as the protector of the Slav peoples, including the Serbs. As protector of the Slavs (Pan-Slavism), Russia moved to support Serbia. That brought Germany, Austria-Hungary's ally, into the crisis.

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. He was killed by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist linked with a secret society, not an officer acting on official orders. Austria-Hungary nevertheless blamed Serbia.

questions.stem_md: How did Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia lead to war within a week?

questions.solution_md: Russia; Germany against Russia and France; Belgium and Britain.

With reference to the outbreak of war in 1914, answer the following.

(i) Why was the Balkan region tense in the years before 1914? **[3]**

questions.solution_md: Balkan tension; the assassination; the chain to general war.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Austria-Hungary** had annexed **Bosnia** in **1908**, angering **Serbia**, which hoped to unite the region's Serbs. **Russia**, the protector of the Slavs, backed Serbia, while **Germany** backed Austria-Hungary, so the Balkans became a meeting point of great-power rivalry.

(ii) **Archduke Franz Ferdinand**, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, and his wife were **shot dead** at **Sarajevo**, the capital of Bosnia, by **Gavrilo Princip**, a young **Bosnian Serb** nationalist.

(iii) Austria-Hungary blamed **Serbia**, sent it an **ultimatum** and declared war on **28 July 1914**. **Russia** mobilised; **Germany** declared war on Russia and **France**, and invaded **Belgium**; **Britain** declared war on **4 August 1914**. The **alliance system** turned a local crisis into a general war.

questions.stem_md: The Treaty of Versailles with Germany was signed on 28 June of which year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1919. It was signed on 28 June 1919, exactly five years after Sarajevo. The armistice ended the fighting in November 1918.

questions.stem_md: Under which article of the Treaty of Versailles was Germany made to accept responsibility for the war?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Article 231, the war-guilt clause. Article 231, the war-guilt clause, placed responsibility for the war and its losses on Germany and its allies. It was the basis for reparations.

questions.stem_md: The payments that Germany was required to make to the Allies for war damage were called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** reparations. Reparations were payments for war damage, linked to the war-guilt clause. Mandates were former colonies placed under other powers.

questions.stem_md: To what size did the Treaty of Versailles limit the German army?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 100,000 men. The German army was limited to 100,000 men, conscription was banned, and Germany was forbidden an air force.

questions.stem_md: What did the Treaty of Versailles decide about the Saar coal-mining region?

options.text_md: It was given permanently to Poland
It was made a free city like Danzig
It was placed under the League of Nations for 15 years, with its coal mines given to France

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It was placed under the League of Nations for 15 years, with its coal mines given to France. The Saar was run by the League of Nations for 15 years, and France received its coal mines; afterwards its people would vote on their future.

questions.stem_md: The German region along the Rhine bordering France was to have no German troops or fortifications. This term of the treaty is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** demilitarisation of the Rhineland. The Rhineland was demilitarised, protecting France from a sudden German attack.

questions.stem_md: A student looking at a schematic map notices that East Prussia is cut off from the rest of Germany after 1919. Which term of the treaty explains this?

options.text_md: The Saar was placed under the League
The Polish Corridor gave Poland a strip of land to the sea, separating East Prussia from Germany

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Polish Corridor gave Poland a strip of land to the sea, separating East Prussia from Germany. The Polish Corridor gave the new Poland access to the Baltic Sea, which separated East Prussia from the rest of Germany. The other terms concern Germany's western border.

questions.stem_md: What happened to Germany's overseas colonies under the peace settlement?

options.text_md: They were returned to Germany after five years
They were taken away and given to the Allies to govern as mandates under the League
They were made into independent states at once
They were sold to the United States

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** They were taken away and given to the Allies to govern as mandates under the League. Germany lost all its colonies. They were placed under Allied powers as mandates supervised by the League of Nations.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes how many Germans regarded the Treaty of Versailles?

options.text_md: As a dictated peace imposed on Germany without negotiation, which they resented
As a generous settlement that left Germany stronger
As a treaty that Germany had written itself
As an agreement that ended reparations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** As a dictated peace imposed on Germany without negotiation, which they resented. Germany was not allowed to negotiate the terms, and many Germans saw the treaty as a dictated peace; this resentment later fed extreme nationalism. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Treaty of Versailles returned Alsace-Lorraine to France.

**Reason (R):** Germany had taken these provinces from France in 1871.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and R explains A: the treaty reversed Germany's gain of 1871 by giving the provinces back to France.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Treaty of Versailles allowed Germany to keep a large air force.

**Reason (R):** The treaty aimed to make Germany too weak to threaten its neighbours.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: Germany was forbidden to have an air force. R is true: the military terms aimed to keep Germany weak.

questions.stem_md: True or false? German delegates took a full part in drafting the terms of the Treaty of Versailles.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The terms were drawn up by the victorious Allies; Germany was presented with them and had to sign.

questions.stem_md: The clause of the Treaty of Versailles that placed responsibility for the war on Germany is known as the war-___ clause.

questions.stem_md: State two military terms imposed on Germany by the Treaty of Versailles.

questions.stem_md: Mention two losses of territory that Germany suffered under the Treaty of Versailles.

1. **Alsace-Lorraine** was returned to **France**.

questions.stem_md: What arrangements did the Treaty of Versailles make for the Saar and for Danzig?

questions.stem_md: Why did many Germans resent the Treaty of Versailles? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It was a **dictated** peace: Germany had **no say** in its terms.
2. The **war-guilt** clause and heavy **reparations**, together with losses of **land** and **colonies**, were seen as **humiliating** and harsh.

questions.stem_md: Classify the terms of the Treaty of Versailles into military, territorial and financial, giving one example of each.

3. **Financial:** Germany had to pay **reparations** for war damage, based on the **war-guilt** clause.

questions.stem_md:
With reference to the Treaty of Versailles, answer the following.

(i) When and where was the treaty signed, and what was the war-guilt clause? **[3]**
(ii) State three territorial terms of the treaty. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the military terms and explain why Germany found the treaty hard to accept. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Date, place, war guilt; territorial terms; military terms and resentment.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The treaty was signed on **28 June 1919** in the **Palace of Versailles**, near Paris. Under the **war-guilt clause** (**Article 231**), Germany had to accept **responsibility** for the war and the losses it caused, which became the basis for **reparations**.

(ii) **Alsace-Lorraine** was returned to **France**. The **Polish Corridor** gave Poland access to the sea, separating **East Prussia** from Germany, and **Danzig** became a **free city** under the League. Germany's **colonies** were given to the Allies as **mandates**.

(iii) The army was limited to **100,000** men, conscription was banned, and Germany was allowed **no air force** and only a **small navy**; the **Rhineland** was **demilitarised**. Germany found the treaty hard to accept because it was **dictated** without negotiation, the **guilt** clause and **reparations** were humiliating, and the loss of land and colonies left a lasting **grievance**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the peace settlement after the First World War.

(i) What did the Allies hope to achieve by the military terms imposed on Germany? **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the arrangements for the Saar and the Rhineland reflected French concerns. **[3]**

questions.solution_md: Aims of military terms; French security; seeds of conflict.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Allies wanted to make Germany **too weak to attack** its neighbours again. Limiting the army to **100,000** men, banning **conscription** and an **air force**, and allowing only a **small navy** were meant to remove its power to wage an offensive war.

(ii) France had been invaded twice in fifty years. Demilitarising the **Rhineland** kept German troops away from the French border, and placing the **Saar** under the **League** for **15 years** with its **coal mines** given to France compensated France for war damage to its own mines.

(iii) Germany saw the treaty as a **dictated peace**; the **war-guilt** clause and **reparations** created bitterness; the **Polish Corridor** and **Danzig** left Germans under foreign rule and became future disputes; and the **League** that was to keep the peace lacked the **USA** and had **no army** of its own.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The idea of an **association of nations** was put forward by **President Woodrow Wilson** of the USA. Its **Covenant** was included in the **peace treaties of 1919**, and the League began work in **January 1920**, with its headquarters at **Geneva**.

(ii) To **maintain peace** through **collective security**; to settle disputes by **arbitration** and **peaceful** means; and to promote **disarmament**, **international cooperation** and fair **conditions of labour**.

questions.stem_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The fighting ended with an **armistice** signed on **11 November 1918**, after Germany's armies were exhausted and its allies had collapsed. The peace terms with Germany were set out in the **Treaty of Versailles**, signed on **28 June 1919**.

(ii) Germany lost **Alsace-Lorraine**, the **Polish Corridor** and all its **colonies**; its army was cut to **100,000** men with **no air force**; and it had to pay **reparations** under the **war-guilt** clause.

(iii) The war had shown the danger of rival **alliances** and the **armament race**. 2. The **long-term causes**—aggressive **nationalism**, **imperialism**, the **armament race** and the **rival blocs**—had already made Europe ready for war.

questions.stem_md: Which country was NOT a member of the Triple Entente?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Germany. Germany belonged to the Triple Alliance; Britain, France and Russia formed the Entente.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Germany and France came into conflict over Morocco in 1905 and 1911.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The two Moroccan crises showed how colonial rivalry raised tension.

questions.stem_md: The young Bosnian Serb who shot the Archduke at Sarajevo was Gavrilo ___.
questions.solution_md: The assassin was Gavrilo Princip.

questions.stem_md: On which date did Britain declare war on Germany?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 4 August 1914. Britain declared war on 4 August 1914, after Germany invaded Belgium.

questions.stem_md: In which palace near Paris was the peace treaty with Germany signed in 1919?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Versailles. The treaty was signed in the Palace of Versailles near Paris.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Treaty of Versailles returned Alsace-Lorraine to France.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Germany had taken the provinces in 1871; the treaty returned them.

questions.stem_md: The headquarters of the League of Nations were at ___.
questions.solution_md: The League was based at Geneva.

questions.stem_md: Which of these powers never became a member of the League of Nations?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the USA. The USA never joined; Britain, France and Japan were founding members.
